text: With $E(x)$: $x$ is an engineer and $K(x)$: $x$ knows Python, which formula says **“every engineer knows Python”**?
solution: “Every engineer” is a universal over a restricted noun, so the restriction becomes the hypothesis of $\to$.
$\forall x\, (E(x) \to K(x))$: for each $x$, if $x$ is an engineer then $x$ knows Python.
Non-engineers keep the promise vacuously, exactly as the English intends.

common_wrong.why: $\forall x\, (E \wedge K)$ claims everyone is an engineer who knows Python.
That is “some engineer knows Python”.
$\exists x\, (E \to K)$ is true as soon as one non-engineer exists.

text: With $F(x)$: $x$ is a fruit and $S(x)$: $x$ is sour, which formula says **“some fruit is sour”**?
solution: “Some fruit” is an existential over a restricted noun: the restriction is joined with $\wedge$.
$\exists x\, (F(x) \wedge S(x))$: one object that is a fruit and sour, both at once.

common_wrong.why: $\exists x\, (F \to S)$ is made true by any non-fruit.
That is “every fruit is sour”.
$\forall x\, (F \wedge S)$ says everything is a sour fruit.

text: The domain is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $y \mid x$ means $y$ divides $x$. For how many $x$ in the domain is $\exists y\, (y \mid x \wedge 1 < y \wedge y < x)$ true?
solution: The formula says $x$ has a divisor strictly between 1 and $x$, i.e. $x$ is composite (with the divisor inside the domain).
1, 2, 3 and 5 have no such divisor. 4 has $y = 2$; 6 has $y = 2$ (and 3).
So the formula is true for $x = 4$ and $x = 6$.
concept: Read a number-theory formula back into its textbook meaning, then test each element.

common_wrong.why: Counting 1 as composite: 1 has no divisor strictly between 1 and 1.
Counting the primes instead of the composites.

text: Which is the negation of $\forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0)$?
solution: Flip each quantifier, keeping the order $x, y$: $\exists x\, \forall y$.
Negate the matrix: $x + y \ne 0$.
Result: $\exists x\, \forall y\, (x + y \ne 0)$.
concept: Negation flips every quantifier and keeps their order.

common_wrong.why: Flips the order of the variables as well; the order never changes.
Flips the quantifiers but leaves the matrix un-negated.
Negates only the matrix.

text: On the domain $\{a, b, c\}$, $R$ holds exactly for $(a, a), (a, b), (a, c), (b, c), (c, c)$. How many of these six sentences are true: $\forall x \forall y R$, $\exists x \exists y R$, $\forall x \exists y R$, $\exists x \forall y R$, $\forall y \exists x R$, $\exists y \forall x R$ (each with matrix $R(x, y)$)?
solution: Draw the grid: row $a$ is T T T, row $b$ is F F T, row $c$ is F F T.
$\forall\forall$: F (cell $(b, a)$). $\exists\exists$: T. $\forall x \exists y$: every row has a T: T. $\exists x \forall y$: row $a$ is full: T.
$\forall y \exists x$: every column has a T (row $a$ is full): T. $\exists y \forall x$: column $c$ is full: T.
Five of the six are true.
concept: Read ∀x∃y along rows, ∃x∀y as a full row, ∀y∃x along columns, ∃y∀x as a full column.

common_wrong.why: Missing that column $c$ is full, so $\exists y\, \forall x$ is true.
Forgetting that $\forall\forall$ needs every cell.

text: With $G(x)$: $x$ is a graduate and $E(x)$: $x$ is eligible, which formula says **“only graduates are eligible”**?
solution: “Only graduates” restricts who can be eligible: anyone eligible must be a graduate.
So: for every $x$, if $x$ is eligible then $x$ is a graduate, $\forall x\, (E(x) \to G(x))$.
concept: “Only A are B” = ∀x (B → A): the arrow reverses.

common_wrong.why: That is “all graduates are eligible”, a different claim.
That only says some eligible graduate exists.
Says everyone is an eligible graduate.

text: Which formulas say that **exactly one** element has property $P$? (Select all that apply.)

options.t: $\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, ((P(x) \wedge P(y)) \to x = y)$

solution: Option A is the standard form: some $x$ has $P$, and every $y$ with $P$ equals $x$.
Option B is “at least one” ∧ “at most one”, the same meaning.
Option C alone is true when **no** element has $P$; option D says at least two.
concept: Exactly one = at least one + at most one.

common_wrong.why: “At most one”: it is true when nothing has $P$.
That is “at least two”.

text: Over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, which sentence is **true**?
solution: B: for any $x$, take $y = x - 1$; then $y < x$. True.
A: any candidate $y$ fails at $x = y$. C: any candidate $x$ fails at $y = x - 1$. D fails at $y = x$.
concept: ∀∃ lets the witness depend on x; ∃∀ needs one witness for all.

common_wrong.why: No integer exceeds every integer (it fails against itself).
$\mathbb{Z}$ has no least element; on $\mathbb{N}$ this would be true.
Fails when $x = y$.

text: On the domain $\{1, 2, 3\}$ with the usual $>$, for how many of the $2^3$ choices of a unary predicate $P$ is $\forall x\, (P(x) \to \exists y\, (y > x \wedge P(y)))$ true?
solution: The sentence says: every element of $P$ has a larger element of $P$.
If $P$ is non-empty, its largest element $m$ needs some $y > m$ in $P$, which is impossible.
So only $P = \varnothing$ works (vacuously). Answer: 1.
concept: A finite non-empty set has a largest element; ‘always a bigger one’ forces emptiness (or an infinite domain).

common_wrong.why: Counting $P = \{1, 2, 3\}$, but its largest element 3 has nothing above it.
Forgetting that the empty predicate makes a ∀x (P(x) → …) vacuously true.
